title: Kinds of taxes
blurb: What taxes are for, sales tax, income tax and capital gains.

levels.title: What taxes are
learn: Name the main kinds of tax in Canada.
Say what each one is charged on.

cards.text: Taxes are payments you must make to a government. They are not a choice. Three levels of government collect taxes: federal, provincial or territorial, and municipal (your city or town).

image.alt: A wooden box with a slot beside gold discs and a blank paper form

cards.text: There are several kinds of tax. Each one is charged on something different. The table shows six of them.

figure.title: Kinds of tax
rows: Most goods and services you buy
Some goods, such as fuel-inefficient vehicles

cards.text: Property taxes are calculated by municipal (local) governments. They are based on the value of land and buildings. Individuals and businesses pay income tax on their income.

image.alt: A small model house and lawn with a measuring tape and a blank paper tag

cards.text: Excise taxes are imposed on fuel-inefficient vehicles, including station wagons, vans and sport utility vehicles, and on gasoline, diesel fuel, aviation gasoline and aviation fuel. Excise duties are charged on spirits, wine, beer, tobacco, cannabis and vaping products.

image.alt: A fuel can, a bottle and a barrel on a shelf, each with a blank label and a gold disc

cards.text: Some taxes come off your pay. CPP and EI contributions come off an employee's pay. CPP is a retirement pension you could receive at 60 or older after at least one valid contribution. EI pays benefits to people who lose their jobs through no fault of their own.

image.alt: A blank pay slip with two gold discs moving toward two plain jars

cards.text: Taxes help pay for education and schools, health care and hospitals, and roads and bridges. The next level looks at the GST, the HST and the PST.

image.alt: A model school, hospital and bridge on a table with a gold disc beside each

levels.title: Sales tax in Canada
learn: Tell the GST, the HST and a PST apart.
Work out sales tax on a purchase.

cards.text: The GST is a federal tax you pay on most goods and services you buy in Canada. The rate is 5%. The CRA rates table shows Alberta with a GST of 5% and a provincial rate of 0%.

image.alt: A shop counter with a wrapped parcel with a blank tag beside a stack of gold discs

cards.text: In some provinces the GST and the provincial tax are combined into one tax, the HST. Nova Scotia's HST rate decreased to 14% on April 1, 2025. The table shows the rates the CRA lists.
Other provinces charge a provincial sales tax (PST) as well as the GST. A PST is a tax some provinces charge. The table shows the GST and provincial rate for each province.
Sales tax is the price times the rate. Say Dev buys headphones for $60.00 in Alberta. The GST is $60.00 x 5% = $3.00. Dev pays $63.00 in all.

image.alt: Headphones on a counter beside a stack of gold discs with one set apart

cards.text: The same price can carry different tax. A jacket costs $80.00 before tax. With the 5% GST in Alberta, the tax is $4.00. With the 13% HST in Ontario, it is $10.40. The difference is $6.40.

image.alt: Two matching jackets with a tall and a short stack of gold discs under them

levels.title: Income tax and capital gains
learn: Say what a capital gain is.
Work out the taxable part of a gain.

cards.text: Individuals and businesses pay taxes on their income. In Canada each person does their own taxes every year. A later unit shows how to fill in a return by hand.

image.alt: A desk with blank sheets, a pencil and a ruler

cards.text: You usually have a capital gain or loss when you sell capital property. It is a gain when you sell for more than the total of its adjusted cost base (ACB) and the outlays and expenses incurred to sell it. In our examples nothing was spent to sell, so the gain is the sale price minus the ACB, what was paid.

image.alt: An open wooden chest of blank certificates beside a large stack of gold discs

cards.text: Only part of a capital gain is taxed. The inclusion rate is the fraction of a gain that counts as income and gets taxed. For 2025 the CRA says the rate is 50%, so half of a gain is taxable.

image.alt: A pie cut in half with a gold disc on one half and a ruler across the plate

cards.text: A change was proposed: raise the rate from one-half to two-thirds on gains over $250,000 a year for individuals. Budget 2025 documents describe the proposed increase as cancelled. Check the year before you use a rate.

image.alt: A blank signpost at a fork with two arrow boards, one struck through with a bar

cards.text: Example. Ana sells shares for $1,200.00. She paid $800.00. Her gain is $400.00. At 50%, $200.00 of it is taxable.

When a person dies, they are considered to have sold all their property just before death. The exception is property transferred to a spouse or common-law partner, or a specific exception that applies.

image.alt: An open door at the end of a hallway with a blank paper and a closed chest on a table
